posts.headline: Founder & CEO of Strativa Web Solution | Selify Nigeria | Software Developer | Building E-commerce and real-world digital products
posts.text: A website without SEO is like opening a beautiful shop in a place nobody knows exists. This one is for the decision-makers in business CEOs, Business Development Managers, HR Managers, Heads of Departments, and business owners. If you’re not in any of these categories, you might want to scroll to the next post. 😊 Just kidding Pull up a chair and stay with me. You’re about to learn something strategic. Let me ask you a simple question. What is the point of having a business website if your potential customers can’t find it? Having a website is a great step towards building your business online. But hiring a developer to build your website and make it live is only the beginning. Here’s where many businesses miss a crucial piece of the puzzle SEO (Search Engine Optimisation). And yes, I’ll say it again. SEO! When hiring a professional to build your website or develop custom business software, don't focus only on the design, features, and delivery timeline. Ask questions about how the solution will help your business get discovered online, where applicable. A website should do more than look good. It should be built with visibility, usability, and business goals in mind. Think about it. You’ve owned a website for five years. Every year, you renew your domain and pay for hosting, but your website has generated no meaningful enquiries, leads, or sales. Of course, not every website is designed to generate direct sales. Some serve other purposes. But if your website is meant to attract customers and support business growth, shouldn't it be contributing to those goals? A website that nobody can find is missing a major part of its potential. This is why I believe website development and SEO should work together from the start, not be treated as completely separate projects. And the opportunity goes beyond traditional search engines. As more people use AI-powered platforms to discover businesses, products, and services, it's also worth considering how your website's content and structure can help these platforms understand your business and its expertise. That’s the approach I bring to my work. I BUILD. I OPTIMISE. I HELP BUSINESSES IMPROVE THEIR ONLINE VISIBILITY. My goal is not just to help you put a website online, but to help you build a stronger digital presence that supports your business objectives. So, if your business has a website that isn't delivering the value you expected, perhaps it's time to look beyond the design and ask the right questions. Let's talk. Send me a message, and let's explore how to make your website work harder for your business.

posts.text: I was waiting a long time to make a post with a new offer in it. Not this time, but here’s what happened instead. 😄 I recently went through the hiring processes at Hevo Data, mthree and Infosys. Each one took me further than I expected and showed me something different about where I stand. Hevo Data (SDE-1, Backend) The role was a great fit and the pay was really good, so this was one I wanted badly. Online assessment with 6 questions. A 2-hour LLD round (a Ride Sharing Application). LLD was new to me, I learned it in a hurry, and I cleared it in C++, which is not the easiest language for it.cleared it Stopped at the manager round, where maybe team fit ig was not there with me, I was almost there. mthree Assessment, then a group discussion where we had to speak on AI. Technical round with 2 Java questions plus SQL. Java was something I had learned recently, and I got through it. I cleared every round but ended up on the waitlist because of limited vacancies. Infosys Round 1 was an online DSA exam, and I solved the questions well enough to move forward. Round 2 was an offline DSA exam in Delhi. I solved it and earned a place in the L1 interview. I cleared the L1 interview and reached the final round. There, the questions were on system design, HLD and the architecture of my own projects. Time was tight, and it showed me how deep I need to go on design decisions, trade-offs and scaling. What I’m taking from this I’m not blaming the companies. The things in my control are my preparation and how I show up, and that is where I’m working. Know your projects at the architecture level. Be ready to explain why you built them the way you did, what the HLD looks like and how they would scale. Time management in interviews is a skill. I’m practicing it with timed mock sessions. Behavioral preparation matters as much as technical preparation. Explaining my decisions and trade-offs clearly is the next thing I’m improving. Learning a new language or topic fast, as I did with Java and LLD, works. It just needs to be paired with depth. Beyond the prep Outside of interviews, I’ve been going to the gym, sleeping properly, keeping a steady routine and updating my skills and resume. All of it helped a lot more than I expected, and it keeps me sharp and calm through the waiting. There has been a bit of luck and a bit of bad luck along the way, but I’m in a good place. I enjoyed these processes, I’m clear on what to improve, and I’m hopeful that something good comes soon. #InterviewExperience #HevoData #mthree #Infosys #SoftwareEngineering #SystemDesign #LowLevelDesign

posts.author: Harish Kumar V
posts.headline: Building "Be Practical" - On a Mission to Create Future Ready Workforce | Founder @Yugyantra Technologies Pvt Ltd
posts.text: Every company wants AI talent. Almost none of them want to build it. Naukri's September data makes this painfully clear: → AI/ML hiring: +20% → Overall white-collar hiring: +1% → Freshers (0–3 yrs): +1% That 20x gap isn't a blip. It's a signal about how the market now works. Look at who's actually winning: Experience Growth 0–3 years +1% 4–7 years −2% 8–12 years +5% 13–15 years +7% 16+ years +5% Mid-level is shrinking. Senior is growing. Entry-level is flat. The market is hollowing out from the middle and rewarding the top. And look at where the growth is: ✅ AI/ML +20% ✅ Auto +11% ✅ BPO/ITES +4% ❌ IT/Software Services −4% ❌ Hospitality −11% ❌ Telecom −12% ❌ Education −18% The irony is brutal: AI is booming inside an IT sector that's shrinking. Same industry, opposite trajectories. The generic developer role is being automated; the AI specialist role is being created. What this actually means: 1. "Learn AI" isn't advice anymore—it's table stakes. The +20% is real, but it's concentrated in people who can build, not people who can talk about AI. This is the same point HCLTech made: exposure ≠ employability. 2. The experience ladder is broken. If 4–7 years is shrinking and 16+ is growing, the rungs in the middle are missing. That's a structural problem companies will feel in a decade. 3. Geography is diversifying. Udaipur +19%, Chandigarh +18%, Amritsar +13%. Meanwhile Delhi-NCR and Mumbai both fell 6%. The old "move to Bengaluru" playbook is outdated. The honest takeaway for freshers: The market isn't closed. It's selective. And "selective" means it rewards specificity, demonstrable skill, and being in the right sector—not a degree and a hope.

posts.author: Chatresh Consultants
posts.text: The Education Gap & the Unspoken Realities of Junior Tech Hiring Why do we treat software engineering education like memorising state capitals? Memorise the syntax. Answer 30 multiple-choice questions. Submit a neat, isolated solo coursework assignment. Get an 'A'. Then that same graduate walks into their very first technical interview or probationary sprint, and the engineering lead asks: • “Walk me through how you resolve a rebase conflict on a team branch.” • “How would you trace an unhandled promise rejection crashing this microservice?” • “Explain the database locking trade-off in your latest project.” Silence. Here is the inconvenient truth that academic curricula and 12-week online video bootcamps rarely address: writing new code is only about 30% of a working software engineer’s job. The other 70% is messy, unpredictable, and social: 1. Digging through legacy code with zero documentation. 2. Formulating the exact technical question to ask when you've been blocked for 45 minutes. 3. Defending design decisions during an architecture review without taking criticism personally. 4. Structuring Pull Requests so your senior colleagues don't reject your branch on sight. You cannot absorb that through passive screen time. Watching an instructor code in a pre-recorded sandbox gives the illusion of competence—until you open an empty terminal on your own machine and nothing works. At the LUYSK (Level Up Your Skills-learning arm of Chatresh Consultants) center in Sevenoaks, Kent, we built a learning model that completely strips out the classroom lecture. When students walk through our doors, they don’t sit in rows looking at slides. They log into a dedicated dual-monitor workstation inside an active engineering room. They join a real morning standup. They take on blocker tickets, whiteboard system data flows with senior developers who build real enterprise systems, and learn the discipline of writing production-grade code. If you want someone to learn how to play football, you don’t keep them in a lecture hall reading the official rulebook. You give them boots and put them on the pitch. Tech education should work the exact same way. To the engineering managers and developers reading this: what was the single biggest shock you faced during your first month working in a real engineering team? Let’s talk about it below. 👇 Website & Experience Passes: luysk.co.uk #TechEducation #SoftwareEngineering #CareerDevelopment #JuniorDeveloper #CodingBootcamp #STEMUK #DevCommunity #LearnToCode

posts.headline: I build intelligent hiring systems & create career opportunities | AI-powered Talent Systems, Hiring Strategy & Transformation, Community Leadership | Founder @The Principal Recruiter & Talent Crunch
posts.text: I put a sign on a wall offering a session on hiring or looking for a job At one point, around 9 people were sitting with me This was during the #unconference part at the t3 cto summit - Software Engineering Leadership last Friday, after my Human API roundtable (shout out to Manjuri) So people brought their questions or ideas or thoughts related to Hiring and / or Job Searches and then we just went through them...it was a lot of: "I will need to make assumptions here" and "Please allow me to simply rapid fire ideas, to save time" - on my part (normally I would have asked them waaaay more questions 👀 It felt like a continuous coaching session 😆 for over 2.5h, and I realised it lasted so long when I stood up and everything in my body hurt 🤭 I loved EVERY minute or it And I realised how much I had missed being around tech and senior people 😫 I spent 16 years in tech or specialist engineering. Spending time again with engineering leaders, founders and people between roles brings me closer to the work I am really good at My roundtable surfaced some questions (another post abt this): • How do you assess technical judgement when candidates use AI? • How do you develop junior engineers when their starting tasks disappear? • How do you recognise good performance when output is easier to produce? Then the unconference brought the conversation directly to individual hiring and career decisions We need more time listening outside our own professional circles! Before producing another hiring framework, workshop or piece of content, ask an <insert profession> leader what they are struggling to assess. Ask someone looking for work where the process loses them Their answers should shape our work, not more of the "wanna be" overnight "gurus" on LinkedIn, some of which gained notoriety because you see their face often (yes, mine included perhaps), and not because they ever did the job properly - but speak to the Re-Le-Vaaaant people!!! Pretty please 🙏 Thank you, Greg Fawson, for having me back. More of this, please 😍

posts.author: Prithviraj Manoharlal Tiwari
posts.headline: ​SITPUNE
posts.text: We need an honest discussion about the current math facing engineering graduates. ​For the past many years where large service firms absorbed entire graduating classes has fundamentally shifted. Routine coding is getting automated, entry-level hiring has contracted, and yet degrees still cost ₹15–25 lakhs across tuition and living expenses. Meanwhile, students spend the majority of their daily bandwidth complying with statutory attendance requirements, assignment submissions, and educational institutions' administrative workings. ​Telling everyone to simply pivot into DevOps, Forward Deployed Engineering, or advanced software architecture is unrealistic. Those roles demand deep specialization, not surface-level certificates. ​If you are a student right now, the time for passive waiting is gone. You essentially have three realistic choices: ​Self-Audit for the Top Tier: Be completely honest with your technical aptitude. If you have the drive and capability to compete at the highest level, commit fully. Go deep into distributed systems, low-level architecture, or specialized domains so you stand out as a specialized engineer for modern engineering teams. ​Embrace the MSME & Early Startup Path: If you realize you fit a more conventional profile, drop the stigma around smaller businesses, MSMEs, operations, and early-stage startups. The initial paycheck will likely be modest, but the hands-on exposure, rapid ownership, and practical problem-solving skills you gain offer a far better long-term upside than waiting for an MNC drive that may never come. ​Ignore the Shift and Proceed as Usual: If you prefer to stick to conventional advice, wait out the market, or bet on legacy placement patterns, that is entirely your prerogative. No judgment—sincerely, good luck with your path. ​The worst place to be right now is in the middle: carrying heavy expectations without a clear strategy.

posts.text: Some of Germany’s most demanding AI engineering challenges happen outside the chatbot. Einige der anspruchsvollsten KI-Engineering-Aufgaben in Deutschland liegen außerhalb von Chatbots… Autonomous mobility is one example. Berlin based Motor Ai is developing Level 4 autonomous driving technology. Its Robotics Software Integration Engineer vacancy offers an interesting view of the work behind that ambition. C++. Linux. ROS2. Sensor interfaces. Build pipelines. Systems integration. The role includes reviewing critical code, resolving interface mismatches and coordinating software releases. These are the details that make an intelligent system work as a whole. The software needs to communicate with sensors. Different components need to work together. Changes need to be reviewed. And engineers need to understand how a problem in one part of the system affects another. From a recruitment perspective, this connects disciplines that are often assessed separately: → C++ Software Engineering → Robotics → ROS2 → Embedded Systems → Sensor Integration → CI/CD → Systems Engineering The wider field also depends on testing and safety expertise. That doesn’t mean one engineer needs to master every discipline. It means hiring teams need to understand where someone can take responsibility. Can they integrate software with hardware? Diagnose problems across components? Help deliver dependable releases? I think this is a particularly interesting opportunity for Germany’s industrial and automotive engineering talent. Experience with physical systems could become increasingly valuable as AI moves into operational environments. The strongest candidate may be someone who understands both the intelligence and the engineering surrounding it. posts.author: Tejinder Sandhu
posts.headline: Founder & CTO @ AUREM · Building AI that ships code not just suggests it.
posts.text: "Only developers can maintain software." That belief is about to get old. Most non-technical founders who build with Lovable, Bolt, Replit or v0 hit the same wall after launch: the demo worked, something breaks, and they have no idea why. They either wait on a freelancer or go back into the builder and hope. Here's what we built instead. Inside ORA, 3 separate AI engineers each independently write a fix for your bug. A 4th model reviews all 3 and picks the best one. Only then does it get saved to your actual GitHub repo — nothing ships without that review, and nothing ships without your approval either. You never read a line of code. You just describe what's wrong in plain English. The one requirement: your app's code needs to be on GitHub. Lovable, Bolt, Replit and v0 all have a GitHub sync — turn it on, connect it to ORA, and you can run your own app without hiring an engineer. Starter plan is $9/month. If you've built something with AI and it's started acting up, I'd genuinely like to hear what broke. Comment below — what tool did you build with, and what went wrong? www.auremcto.com #VibeCoding #NoCode #BuildInPublic #IndieHacker #SoloFounder #GitHub

posts.headline: Connecting Science, Business and AI to Create Real-World Impact | Founder, PiBTC and LSCI | Supporting Leaders, Companies and Future Talent
posts.text: Most companies chase the newest tool. The best companies master approaches. Over years across Pharma, MedTech, and Healthcare, I keep seeing the same mistake. Organizations ask: Should we implement AI? Should we adopt Lean? Should we buy this software? Wrong questions. The most successful organizations ask something entirely different. What approach will help us consistently deliver better outcomes? Let us look at what actually works in the real world. Case 1: GE and Six Sigma. When Jack Welch scaled Six Sigma, it was never just a quality initiative. It became an operating system. Decisions became data driven. Improvement stopped being a project and became the culture. Case 2: Medtronic in Hyderabad. Building a massive R&D footprint wasn't just about hiring smart engineers. It required structured processes that enable innovation at scale. Without process discipline, great tech just creates expensive noise. Case 3: Siemens Healthineers. Colocating manufacturing and R&D in Bengaluru to bring products to market faster. That is classic process thinking. Optimize the entire value stream, not just isolated departments. Case 4: Pharma Quality Culture. The shift from reactive quality control to proactive quality culture. Because preventing a defect always beats fixing one after it hits the market. Here is what leaders eventually realize. Technology changes constantly. Approaches endure. If you want to advance fast in Life Sciences and MedTech, stop collecting tools and certificates. Master the fundamentals: Process thinking Root cause analysis Systems design Continuous improvement Change leadership Because the framework that actually works is simple: Problem first. Process second. People third. Technology last. Looking back at your career, what had the bigger impact on your growth? A specific tool or software? Or a problem solving approach that completely changed how you think? Drop your thoughts below. #LifeSciences #Pharma #MedTech #SixSigma #Lean #ContinuousImprovement #Leadership #Healthcare #Strategy

posts.headline: Visit website
posts.text: When we hire developers today, "how fast can you write code?" is no longer the question that matters most. AI tools can generate a working function in seconds. What they can't do is decide whether that function should exist at all. So here is what we pay closer attention to now: → Can you read code you didn't write? Most real work is understanding an existing system, not starting fresh. Reviewing AI-generated code is the same skill. → Do you ask about the requirement before the solution? The best candidates ask "who uses this and what problem does it solve?" before choosing a framework. → Can you explain a trade-off in plain language? Our clients are clinic owners, school administrators and founders. If you can't explain why something takes two weeks, the project gets harder for everyone. → Do you know when something is wrong? Spotting a security gap, a slow query or a missing edge case is worth more than writing extra lines. → Do you take ownership after launch? Software lives for years. The people who care about how it behaves in month six are the ones we want on the team. For junior developers, this is good news. You don't need to know every tool. You need to understand problems clearly, keep learning, and get comfortable reviewing and testing, not just generating. Developers and hiring managers: what skill do you think matters more now than it did five years ago? #SoftwareDevelopment #Hiring #DeveloperCareers #TechTeams #AI

posts.author: Lakshay Singhal
posts.headline: Senior Software Development Engineer at Be10x
posts.text: Everyone is saying software engineering is finished. But one perspective from a Google Engineering Manager with nearly 20 years in tech suggests that what’s really changing is the role of the engineer—not the need for engineers. AI isn't replacing software engineers overnight. It is changing what engineers need to be good at. 1. Coding is changing, not disappearing The value is shifting toward problem-solving, architecture, edge cases, and understanding the customer. 2. We're entering the agentic era AI can now handle increasingly complex tasks, but giving it a completely new real-world problem and expecting it to independently understand context and own the outcome is still a much higher bar. 3. Fresher hiring will get harder "I know Java + LeetCode" won't be enough. Engineers will need to show they can build with AI, question its output, and take ownership of what ships. 4. CS fundamentals still matter Focus on: → DSA → OS & Networks → Distributed Systems → System Design → Problem Solving 5. Interviews will evolve Expect more questions like: → Debug AI-generated code → Find security issues → Scale a system → Review an AI solution The question shifts from "Can you write code?" to "Can you judge code?" 6. Teams won't necessarily shrink dramatically The same team may simply become far more productive, with more emphasis on senior-level thinking and decision-making. 7. Human value moves toward judgment Business context. Trade-offs. Collaboration. Ownership. When production breaks, someone still needs to understand the problem and own the fix. 8. Learn fundamentals before relying on AI Code without AI first. Understand how systems work. Then use AI aggressively—as a partner, not a replacement for understanding. 9. If you learn only 3 things this year: → Agentic workflows → Systems + data architecture → Business understanding The future of software engineering may not be about writing less code. It may be about thinking better about the code AI helps you write. posts.author: Hasnat Awan, AMIMechE
posts.headline: Graduate Mechanical Engineer at Southern Water
posts.text: Graduate jobs aren’t simply “disappearing because of AI” — but the skills employers expect from graduates are changing fast. A UK government analysis published this year found that overall UK hiring was 14% lower year-on-year in April 2026. Among the entry-level occupations it tracked, Accountant roles were down 29% and Software Engineer roles were down 27%. In total, 30 of the 38 entry-level occupations analysed had seen hiring decline. That sounds worrying — especially if you are graduating into tech, finance or another competitive professional field. But the picture is more complicated than “AI has taken the graduate jobs.” The Institute of Student Employers’ 2026 research found that 87% of employers expect AI to reshape graduate and apprentice roles over the next three years. Importantly, employers generally expect roles to be changed rather than simply replaced. And new Skills England research published in October shows that demand still exists in important areas: software development, IT business analysis and several engineering occupations appear repeatedly as priority skills across UK growth sectors. In digital and technology, around 68% of priority occupations are considered to be in critical or elevated demand, while the equivalent figure in financial services is around 70%. So what is changing? Employers increasingly want graduates who can work beyond routine tasks. In tech, AI is shifting value towards verification, judgement and communication; in finance, it is transforming analytics, fraud detection and risk; and engineering demand remains strong across areas such as clean energy, advanced manufacturing and defence. The goal is not simply to become an “AI expert” — it is to combine your profession with practical AI literacy and strong human judgement. For international graduates, this matters even more because sponsorship adds another filter to an already competitive market. Your application needs to show what you can contribute, not just that you have a degree and need sponsorship. Whether you are in finance, software or engineering, combine your technical skills with data, AI literacy, problem-solving and communication. And remember: a government “priority occupation” is not automatically sponsorable immigration eligibility still needs to be checked separately. My takeaway for graduates entering the 2026/27 market is simple: don’t try to compete with AI at the repetitive tasks it can increasingly perform. Build the skills that make you valuable alongside it judgement, verification, problem-solving, technical depth, communication and the ability to apply technology to real business problems. posts.headline: Experienced technologist. AI Pragmatist | Web3 | E-Commerce | Angel Investor
posts.text: Last month, 24th August. I was on a panel at DevOps Summit Singapore. And the topic: the socio-technical architecture of software-enabled organisations. The point I kept coming back to was this. With AI writing more of the code, the engineer's job moves to specification, verification and orchestration, a point that my fellow panelist Abhik Roychoudhury mentioned when he said that verification and validation is now more important than ever. In my team at Mighty Jaxx, that is already how we work, from using MCP servers for Figma to Shopify code to QA agents. But the code was never the hard part. Someone still has to say exactly what we want, and check that what comes back is correct. That also raises a question which I care about: where do junior engineers learn if AI takes the entry-level tasks? I don't have a full answer yet. But hiring, mentoring and giving interns real work is a good place to start. And interns are expected to be given knottier problems to solve much sooner and the acceleration along the learning curve will accelerate. Now is in fact, a great time to be a software developer as demand will outpace supply It was a session of good questions and great conversations. Thanks to everyone who came by to chat after the session. And thanks to my panel host Sergiu Bodiu and my fellow panelists Albert Xu Ray Booysen and Abhik Roychoudhury for a great discussion. #DevOpsSummitSG #DevOps #AI #EngineeringLeadership

posts.text: Companies are opening more roles, not fewer. If AI were replacing engineers, hiring activity would be dropping, but the demand for developer talent remains active. If anyone can build software with AI, what exactly are companies hiring developers for? AI makes writing code fast, letting teams spin up basic templates and small features in seconds. But writing more code does not equal a working system. When teams rely on AI to write code without careful checking, they get stuck with messy code, hidden bugs, and serious security risks. This is why companies keep hiring developers. They are not looking for someone to type out basic code—AI already does that. They need engineers who understand how different systems connect, how to keep data secure, and how to fix complex problems when things break down. Writing code is cheap now. Good engineering judgment is what companies are actually paying for. #SoftwareEngineering #AI #TechHiring #BackendDevelopment #TechLeadership

posts.text: Why you should learn the full robotics software stack, not just one tool Are you an entry-level Robotics Software Engineer, or a student who has built a few robot projects? Here is a hard truth. Most robots that work in a demo fail in the real world. The reason is rarely the hardware. It is the software around it. Recruiters hiring for robotics roles in 2026 look for people who understand how the pieces connect. Here is what that stack looks like, and why each layer matters: 🔹 ROS 2: The backbone of modern robots. Nodes, topics, services and launch files are how real robot systems talk to each other. If you know ROS 2 well, you can join almost any robotics team. 🔹 Simulation (Gazebo, Isaac Sim): Test before you break hardware. A digital twin lets you stream LiDAR, cameras and IMU data and try out ideas safely. It is also where most industry testing happens now. 🔹 State estimation and perception: Sensors are noisy. Fusing them into one reliable pose, and turning a camera feed into a target, is what separates a toy from a robot you can trust. 🔹 SLAM and Navigation (Nav2): Mapping a space, planning a route and avoiding people and obstacles. This is core to warehouse, logistics and service robotics. 🔹 Manipulation (MoveIt 2): Motion planning for robot arms. Locate, pick, deliver. This is where many Physical AI jobs are heading. 🔹 Testing and failure analysis: The skill nobody teaches. Real engineers inject faults on purpose (sensor dropout, blocked paths, slipped grasps), measure what breaks, and fix it with evidence. Tracking error, latency, localisation drift, mission success rate. Numbers, not opinions. 💡 The takeaway: Do not learn these as separate tutorials. Build one robot and keep adding to it, layer by layer, until it runs a full autonomous mission. That is the project that gets you hired. 🎓 This is how we built the Quanskill Robotics Systems Level 2 course. It is 12 weeks online, one robot with a new skill every week, and strong graduates move on to a 3-month internship with QuanRobotics. The first batch starts in November, and each batch has only 10 seats. The application link is in the comments. 📚 References: ROS 2: docs.ros.org Gazebo: gazebosim.org Nav2: nav2.org MoveIt 2: moveit.ros.org Isaac Sim: https://lnkd.in/gSm6qef7 Which layer of the stack do you find hardest? posts.text: Hello everyone! 👋✨ Many of you have been asking me how to prepare for Infosys, what the recruitment process looks like, which subjects to focus on, and how I got selected. So, here it is — the long-awaited post! 💙 First of all, apologies to all my peers, fellow graduates, and soon-to-be graduates who are in the final days of their college journey for keeping you waiting! HOW TO GET INTO INFOSYS AS A FRESHER? 💻 Recruitment Process | Exam Pattern | Preparation Strategy Lets break it down. 👇 1️⃣ How can you get into Infosys? -On-campus: Through your college placement drive. -Off-campus: Apply through official Infosys career opportunities. -Specialized hiring: Explore roles such as Specialist Programmer (SP) and Digital Specialist Engineer (DSE), which generally require stronger technical skills. 2️⃣ What is the recruitment process? The process varies by role and hiring drive, but it may include: Round 1: Online Assessment -Quantitative aptitude -Logical reasoning -Verbal ability -Programming fundamentals and pseudocode -Coding questions, depending on the role Round 2: Technical Interview -Programming fundamentals and DSA -OOP, DBMS and SQL -Operating Systems and Computer Networks -Projects and resume-based questions Round 3: HR/Managerial Discussion -Self-introduction and career goals -Strengths and weaknesses -Relocation and situational questions Always check the official instructions for your specific hiring drive. 3️⃣ What should you prepare? 📌 Aptitude: Percentages, ratios, averages, time and work, probability. 📌 Reasoning: Puzzles, series, arrangements and data interpretation. 📌 Verbal: Grammar, vocabulary and reading comprehension. 📌 Programming: Build a strong foundation in C++, Java or Python. 📌 Core CS: OOP, DBMS, SQL, OS, CN and DSA. 📌 Coding: Arrays, strings, sorting, searching, recursion and other role-relevant problems.📌 Projects: Understand your implementation, technologies and contribution thoroughly. 4️⃣ My personal advice ❤️ You don't need to master everything in a week. Start with the basics, practise consistently, and focus on understanding concepts rather than memorizing answers. For SP and DSE roles, strengthen your coding and problem-solving skills. For technical interviews, confidence backed by conceptual clarity is essential. Dont prepare just to secure an offer letter. Prepare to become someone who can solve problems, communicate clearly and learn independently. Your first job doesn't define your entire career. Let it be the beginning of your growth. 🚀 In pictures: This wasn.t just a building; it was a place that shaped us as individuals. 💙✨ #Infosys #Freshers #CampusPlacements #PlacementPreparation #CareerGuidance #ITJobs #DSA

posts.text: 1,000 junior tech jobs are never publicly posted. That's right. Many entry-level roles get filled through direct connections, referrals, or before they even hit major job boards. For new grads, interns, and career changers, this means you need to go beyond just applying online. You need to find the people who are actually hiring. Here's a LinkedIn search hack to uncover these hidden opportunities and connect with the right decision-makers: 1. Go to LinkedIn's main search bar. 2. Type your desired role (e.g., "Junior Software Engineer"). 3. Click on the "People" filter, then "All filters." 4. Now, for your secret weapon filters: a. "Title": Add terms like "Engineering Manager," "Director of Engineering," "Hiring Manager," "Head of Talent." b. "Current Company": Input specific companies you want to work for. c. "Location": Target your desired cities or regions. d. "Industry": Narrow down to "Computer Software," "Information Technology," etc. 5. Hit "Show results." You'll now see profiles of people directly responsible for building tech teams. Look at their "Posts" section for direct hiring announcements. Check their "About" section for interests or open roles. Send a personalized connection request. Reference something specific from their profile or a company project. This isn't just about finding a job; it's about building relationships that lead to your first tech opportunity. HireMe helps you find junior roles. This helps you get noticed by the right people. posts.text: New grad software engineers at top proprietary trading firms are securing $400,000 to $650,000 in first-year compensation. While enterprise SaaS and consumer tech hiring has normalized, an elite corridor of quantitative trading desks and high-throughput financial rails has decoupled completely from the broader tech labor market. Here is what the empirical numbers and architecture reveal: 1. THE CAPITAL & VOLATILITY FLYWHEEL Unlike enterprise software companies relying on corporate IT budget renewals, automated market makers monetize trading volume and volatility directly: • Jane Street generated a record $39.6B in net trading revenue in 2025 ($16.1B in Q1 2026 alone), averaging over $11M in revenue per employee. • Citadel Securities achieved $9.7B in 2024 net trading revenue (+55% YoY) and $5.2B in EBITDA, executing ~20% of all US equity volume. • Hudson River Trading and Two Sigma continue deploying tens of thousands of cores to capture microscopic statistical arbitrage. 2. FROM HEURISTICS TO ML-DRIVEN ALPHA High-frequency market making is shifting from manual C++ heuristics to automated deep learning on order book dynamics: • High-capacity transformers and temporal convolutional networks running inference on nanosecond-level limit order books. • FPGA pipelines, custom kernel bypass (DPDK/Solarflare), and sub-microsecond tick-to-trade execution. • Real-time feature engineering operating on petabytes of Level 3 market data every trading day. 3. THE DISTRIBUTED LEDGER & FINTECH SCALE ENGINE At infrastructure giants like Stripe, the engineering challenge shifts from microsecond latency to zero-loss consistency: • Processing trillions of dollars in annualized volume at 99.999% availability. • Strong multi-region ledger consistency, immutable state engines, and automated fraud-defense models. The talent bar in this sector has never been higher: modern quant engineering demands a rare intersection of systems mastery (C++, Linux kernel bypass, cache coherence), statistical modeling, and deep ML foundations. posts.text: 1969. Houston, United States. A team of scientists and engineers is preparing a mission that will take human beings to the Moon. Among them is a remarkable woman: Margaret Hamilton, Director of the Software Engineering Division for the Apollo programme. At the time, software engineering is still an emerging discipline. Yet Hamilton understands something fundamental: The success of a complex project does not depend on one individual, but on the ability to bring different areas of expertise together. She champions rigour, anticipates potential failures and insists on preparing for the unexpected. During the Apollo 11 mission, computer overload alarms threaten the lunar landing. But the software has been designed to prioritise critical tasks, allowing the crew to continue their mission. This achievement is no stroke of luck. It is the result of collective effort, clear vision and trust in the expertise of others. Her story offers a powerful management lesson: You can lead a complex project without being the person who knows every technical detail. Even today, some managers believe they must be the most competent person on their team. What a mistake! Hiring someone more talented than you is not a threat. Listening to your colleagues is not a sign of weakness. Surrounding yourself with strong personalities does not diminish your authority. Acknowledging your limitations does not undermine your leadership. A mediocre manager wants to be the smartest person in the room. A great manager wants to bring the smartest minds around the table. Shine on ✨
